title: An open-source semi-automated workflow for multi-omics sample extraction
authors: Hall, D. R.; Trejo, J. B.; Bredeweg, E. L.; Tate, K. L.; Eder, J. G.; Lalli, P. M.; Piehowski, P.; Liu, T.; Shishkov, O.; DeSousa, K.; Gritsenko, M. A.
abstract: Multiomics analysis relies on extracting metabolites lipids and proteins from a single sample A widely used method for this is Metabolomics Proteomics and Lipidomics Extraction MPLEx a triphasic chloroform methanol water extraction but it is manually intensive and depends on skilled operators working around a fragile protein layer Here we present OpenMPLEx a semi automated MPLEx workflow for low cost open source Opentrons liquid handlers A minor change in chemistry pellets the protein so that a robot can collect the aqueous and organic phases from above We compared the automated workflow with two manual MPLEx protocols by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry LC MS based proteomics lipidomics and metabolomics The methods were roughly equivalent and measured similar differences between growth media We then scaled the workflow to 96 well plates and tested it on an 80 sample Pseudomonas putida experiment One operator took all 80 samples from cell pellets to LC MS data in a working week with about 3 h of hands on time rather than days at the bench and quantified about 3 900 protein groups All scripts labware definitions and print files are open source so that other laboratories can adapt the workflow

title: Single-dose neonatal gene therapy preserves motor coordination and extends survival of Polg-deficient mice
authors: Zanin, S.; Moriceau, S.; Afram, E.; Perez-Cartier, M. T.; Gaborit, C.; Simon Sola, M.; Kneeland, S. C.; Murray, S. A.; Munnich, A.; Ruzzenente, B.; Metodiev, M. D.
abstract: POLG mutations are the most common single nuclear gene cause of mitochondrial disease. POLG disease spans a spectrum of clinical presentations with variable age of onset and severity. Early-onset disease is often severe and fatal (e.g., Alpers syndrome, myocerebrohepatopathy), while late-onset disease can be relatively mild (e.g., progressive external ophthalmoplegia). POLG disease is incurable, with few symptomatic treatments available, none of which can prevent its progression. Gene replacement therapy has the potential to halt or prevent POLG disease, but its development has been hindered by the large size of the POLG cDNA and the scarcity of suitable mouse models. Here, we developed a bespoke Polg knockout (KO) mouse model by inactivating the Polg locus in parvalbumin-expressing neurons (e.g., Purkinje cells) and fast-twitch skeletal muscle fibers. KO mice developed progressive motor coordination deficits, respiratory chain deficiency in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, and died prematurely. We also developed nine AAV-based gene therapy vectors and confirmed their ability to deliver and express the human POL{gamma}A protein in different mouse tissues. A single high-dose administration of either of two lead candidates into Polg KO neonates preserved respiratory chain activity in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, delayed the onset of motor coordination deficits, and extended lifespan. Thus, our work provides preclinical proof of concept for gene replacement therapy for POLG disease, establishing the feasibility of this approach and laying the foundation for further development in the field.

title: Convergent Genomic Signatures of Selection in Thar: Genetic trade-offs for desert survival
authors: Rathod, S. M.; Jain, R.; Mukerji, M.
abstract: Background: Desert environments provide a setting for natural biological experiments to cope up with simultaneous stressors of extreme temperatures, aridity, UV exposure, and limited food resources. Biological adaptations that support living in such an environment could become liabilities when the environment and lifestyle change due to gene-environment mismatch. We explored whether genetically and culturally diverse endogamous native populations of the Thar exhibit convergent signatures of selection to desert conditions and whether the selected loci have implications in traits and disease susceptibilities relevant to non-native transitions. Results: We report 348 high-confidence variants across 45 candidate genes from a study on 176 individuals from eight genetically distinct Thar populations. These genes identified from humans and other desert inhabitants display convergent evolution with multiple selection scans (PBSn1, Tajima`s D, iHS, and XPEHH) in diverse Thar populations. Prominent genes include ZNF385D, SGCZ, SARDH, SLC12A3, etc. Selected variants essential in the desert environment were associated with complex traits like lipid metabolism, hypertension, renal and cardiovascular diseases, and addiction in GWAS and PheWAS. Noteworthy, in a syntenic locus, eQTLs in SARDH, which modulates DBH implicated in addiction, suggest a potential link with survival advantage in an uncertain desert environment. Likewise, a selected variant (rs7204044) in SLC12A3, implicated in hypertension in non-desert populations, seems to be a key to water-salt homeostasis in desert natives. Conclusions: These findings suggest that variants linked to adaptive traits in desert conditions could be linked to maladaptation in an altered environment. This has potential health consequences in climatic and lifestyle transitions among native inhabitants.

title: SAM-Dependent Precursor Peptide Engagement by Darobactin Maturase DarE
abstract: Radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) enzymes that synthesize structurally constrained ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) with therapeutic potential mostly do so by employing a dedicated RiPP recognition element (RRE). With the growing number of RRE-free maturases discovered, how these enzymes engage their substrates remains largely unexplored. In this work, we mapped substrate-enzyme interactions in DarE, an RRE-free radical SAM enzyme that installs the C-C and C-O-C crosslinks of the antibiotic darobactin during the first step of darobactin biosynthesis. Using anaerobic hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS), we simultaneously resolved specific regions within the enzyme and its precursor peptide substrate, DarA, across five complex states. The N-terminal extension and part of the TIM-barrel domain of DarE, along with the leader region of DarA, become protected, revealing the peptide-engagement interface. Additional protection emerged only in the presence of SAM, identifying SAM as a key contributor to precursor-peptide engagement in an RRE-free RiPP maturase. Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy further demonstrated precursor peptide-dependent perturbations of the chemical environment of the iron-sulfur clusters. These findings suggest that SAM-dependent peptide engagement, mediated in part by the N-terminal extension of the radical SAM enzyme, provides an alternative mechanism for precursor-peptide recognition in RRE-free RiPP maturases. Our work also demonstrates the utility of anaerobic HDX-MS for characterizing protein-peptide-small molecule interactions in oxygen-sensitive metalloenzymes.

title: Glycoform Distributions and Heparan Sulfate Binding of Intact SARS-CoV-2 Spike Variants by DIA-ECCR Native Mass Spectrometry
authors: Xu, Z.; Du, C.; Olmedillas, E.; Saphire, E. O.; Wysocki, V.
abstract: Glycosylation influences the structure, immunogenicity, and evolutionary selection of the SARS CoV 2 spike protein (S), but its extensive heterogeneity has hindered characterization of intact glycoform distributions. Here, we illustrate a data-independent analysis - electron capture charge reduction (DIA-ECCR) native mass spectrometry workflow for direct analysis of intact spike glycoforms across multiple variants. DIA-ECCR resolves variant-dependent differences in glycoform distributions and higher mass subpopulations. Monte Carlo simulations based on published site-specific bottom-up glycoproteomic data reproduce the central mass of the D614G experimental distribution and support a connection between intact and bottom-up measurements, while the broader experimental distributions and a second Gamma subpopulation indicate heterogeneity not captured by the simulations Mass photometry and charge detection mass spectrometry provide orthogonal measurements consistent with the DIA-ECCR results. DIA-ECCR also resolves mass shifts associated with binding of truncated heparan sulfate, demonstrating analysis of a heterogeneous protein:ligand complex. Together, these results outline a practical workflow that combines DIA-ECCR with native mass spectrometry (nMS) for characterizing intact glycoform distributions and ligand binding in highly heterogeneous glycoprotein assemblies, with potential applications in antigen characterization, vaccine design, and biopharmaceutical quality control.

title: Crystal structure of the first de novo designed phosphotriesterase ZAPP-1
authors: Woodbury, S. M.; Kim, D.; Mendoza, J.; Kang, A.; Nguyen, H.; Bera, A. K.; Baker, D.
abstract: Designing a de novo phosphotriesterase requires scaffolding a dinuclear metal center bound by six catalytic residues, including a post-translationally carbamylated lysine, in a pocket that must also bind a small, flexible organophosphate and orient it for hydrolysis. We recently met this challenge using RFdiffusion3 to design the first de novo phosphotriesterases, and biochemically characterized our first hit, ZAPP-1 [1]. Here we report two crystal structures of ZAPP-1 at 1.42 and 2.28 [A] resolution. The crystal structures are nearly identical to the design model scaffold (C RMSD = 0.69, 0.71, and 0.99 [A] for three copies across two independent crystals), and the higher-resolution crystal assembles the dinuclear Zn(II) site in the designed pocket with carbamylated K16. The catalytic residues are near the designed geometry but demonstrate flexibility across the structures, albeit mostly rotameric (C{beta} RMSD [≤] 0.8 [A] for both copies in form 1). AlphaFold3 predicts the designed catalytic conformation with substrate bound and the observed crystallographic deviations without it, suggesting an induced-fit mechanism upon substrate binding. Together with prior biochemical characterization, there is strong evidence that ZAPP-1 functions as designed, validating the high precision achievable with our RFdiffusion3 design pipeline, but the structures suggest that future design should better preorganize the active site. The ability to design experimentally accurate and increasingly sophisticated enzymes directly from the computer should enable a new future of programmable catalysis and chemistry.

title: Multi-Layer Functional Metabolomics Reveals Chemical Interactions Between the Plant-Associated Bacterium Serratia marcescens and Phytophthora
authors: Herrera Rosero, D.; Geibel, C.; Waqas, M.; Gross, H.; Mordhorst, S.; Petras, D.
abstract: Oomycete pathogens of the genus Phytophthora cause devastating crop losses worldwide, highlighting the need for novel biocontrol agents. Here, we developed a multi-layer functional metabolomics workflow that incorporates an LC-MS/MS-based metal infusion assay in combination with microfractionation-based bioassays against Phytophthora infestans and metal-binding assays to map bioactivity from Serratia marcescens extracts. MS/MS analysis and feature-based molecular networking supported the annotation of activity-associated metabolites, including prodigiosin, serratiochelins, and an uncharacterized putative serratiochelin analog designated serratiochelin G. Complementary chrome azurol S assays and post-column iron infusion provided evidence of iron-binding properties. Comparative genomic analysis and L-lysine supplementation supported a proposed biosynthetic origin of serratiochelin G involving cadaverine incorporation. This workflow enables metabolite prioritization by integrating non-targeted LC-MS/MS with chromatographically resolved bioactivity and complementary functional assays.

title: Mechanistic Insights into ADAR1-p110 Nuclear Import: A Dual-Interface Interaction with Transportin-1
authors: Chin, D. H. R.; Zhou, J.; Luo, Y.; Hong, D.; Tan, Y. B.; Chen, P. L.; Luo, D.
abstract: The human ADAR1 exists as two isoforms: the predominantly cytoplasmic-localized p150, recognized for its role in suppression of aberrant immune activation, and the predominantly nuclear-localized p110 (missing the N terminal Z domain), whose biological functions remain less understood but are thought to rely heavily on its subcellular localization. Despite its structural similarity to the Z domain unique to ADAR1-p150, the functional significance of the Z{beta} domain shared by both isoforms remains unclear. Here, we identify an additional mechanism contributing to the nuclear import of ADAR1-p110 through a dual-interface interaction with transportin-1 (TNPO1), involving both the Z{beta} and dsRBD3 domains of ADAR1. Using cryo-electron microscopy, we show that Z{beta} engages TNPO1 at its canonical cargo-binding groove, while dsRBD3 binds at a peripheral site overlapping the RanGTP binding interface. Structure-guided mutagenesis and biochemical analyses support the contribution of Z{beta} to TNPO1 recognition. Disruption of the interaction between ADAR1 Z{beta} domain and TNPO1 alters the nucleocytoplasmic distribution of ADAR1-p110, resulting in increased cytoplasmic accumulation despite the retention of the previously characterized dsRBD3-associated nuclear localization signal. Furthermore, cytoplasmic redistribution of ADAR1-p110 mutants is accompanied by global suppression of cytosolic innate immune signaling pathways and reduced expression of interferon-stimulated genes. Together, these findings identify ADAR1 Z{beta} as an additional TNPO1-recognition element synergizing with dsRBD3 that contributes to ADAR1-p110 nuclear localization and highlight the relationship between its subcellular distribution and immune regulatory activity.

title: nf-core/pairgenomealign: a scalable pipeline for pairwise whole-genome alignment
authors: Plessy, C.; Mahdi, M.; Fujita, T.; Frith, M. C.; Luscombe, N. M.
abstract: Genome assemblies are accumulating rapidly across the Tree of Life, creating a growing need for reproducible and scalable methods for whole-genome comparison. We developed nf-core/pairgenomealign, a Nextflow workflow that automates pairwise genome alignment using the LAST software suite and produces standard alignment, visualisation, and summary outputs. The pipeline supports a wide range of evolutionary distances, runs reproducibly across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments, and exports alignments in formats including MAF, BAM, BCF, and CRAM. We repurposed the compact format used for sequencing reads to combine the alignments of many genomes to the same target into a single file, which genome browsers display directly and from which multiple sequence alignments of any region can be extracted. Benchmarking against established genome aligners shows competitive performance with tunable trade-offs between speed and sensitivity, while applications to comparative genomics and assembly quality control illustrate its uses.

title: Spinal Recurrent Inhibition Shapes the Dynamics of TMS-induced Motor-Evoked Potentials
authors: Chien, V. S. C.; Bernasconi, E.; Müller, E.; Wang, P.; Lowery, M.; Liegey, J.; Wendt, K.; O'Shea, J.; Denison, T.; Ranieri, F.; Lazzaro, V. D.; Hlinka, J.; Knösche, T. R.; Weise, K.; Schmidt, H.
abstract: Background: Motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) elicited by TMS reflect the integrity of the corticospinal pathway, yet the contributions of spinal and peripheral mechanisms to the shape of individual MEP waveforms remain poorly understood. Objective: To develop a biologically grounded model of the spinal and peripheral motor pathway that can be fitted to individual MEP waveforms across TMS intensities, and to test whether Renshaw cell (RC) recurrent inhibition is required to reproduce them. Methods: Corticospinal volleys (D- and I-waves), reconstructed from published epidural recordings in humans, drove 100 conductance-based leaky integrate-and-fire alpha motor neurons coupled to an RC population. Motor unit action potentials were derived from a finite-element hand model informed by diffusion tensor imaging of the first dorsal interosseous muscle. Models with (RC+) and without (RC-) recurrent inhibition were fitted to MEPs across TMS intensities in 10 healthy participants and compared with a phenomenological benchmark. Results: The RC+ model explained approximately 90% of waveform variance (mean R2 = 0.89), comparable to the benchmark (0.91; p = 0.32). Removing RC inhibition reduced waveform goodness-of-fit in every participant (mean R2 = 0.79; p = 0.002 vs. RC+), although input-output curve fits of MEP amplitude did not differ significantly between the two variants (p = 0.49). Conclusions: RC recurrent inhibition was required to reproduce the temporal structure of TMS-evoked MEPs. MEP waveforms thus carry more information than amplitude-based measures. Fitted to individual waveforms, the model can estimate unobservable spinal and peripheral activity, such as motor unit firing times, as well as participant-specific pathway parameters.

title: Unified CEBRA learns shared neural latents across recordings to map single-neuron contributions to population codes
authors: Benquet, C.; Mirzaeri, H.; Schneider, S.; Mathis, M. W.
abstract: Neural computation is thought to rely on distributed populations; however, most single recording samples capture only a fraction of them, and rare cell types may contribute only a small proportion of neurons per session. Pooling many recordings could reveal how these populations encode information, but each recording samples different neurons, so their contributions cannot be easily compared directly. Here we show that recordings can be combined into a single model of all recorded neurons by aligning them with a shared label, used at both training and inference, placing every neuron's contribution to the population code on a common scale. This approach, called Unified CEBRA, retained interpretable task information across recordings in the monkey and mouse sensorimotor cortex, rat hippocampus, and mouse visual cortex. Pooling thousands of excitatory and inhibitory neurons from hundreds of sessions from mouse visual cortex, we found that the neurons that contributed most to the model's readout of visual features were not only the most strongly tuned, but also those that responded more reliably and were less coupled to co-recorded neurons. Unified CEBRA, therefore, can unveil coding principles studied at the population scale with mappable features to individual neurons from sparse, multi-session recordings using our new approach.

title: Dissociable patterns of neurophysiological alterations during guided search in schizophrenia and autism: Evidence from fixation-related potentials, alpha modulation, and functional MRI.
authors: Gonzalez-Moreira, E.; Martinez, A.; Aburto-Ponce, M. B.; Greisberg, M.; Beggel, O.; Tobe, R. H.; Franco, A. R.; Dias, E.; Javitt, D. C.
abstract: Schizophrenia (SZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are associated with convergent differences in social perception relative to non-autistic, non-schizophrenia controls (NC), but divergent patterns of alterations in early visual activity. Here, we used multimodal imaging during the Guided Visual Search task to investigate the differential patterns of early visual alteration across SZ and ASD including superior colliculus (SC) and pulvinar nucleus. In Experiment 1, simultaneous eye tracking and EEG were obtained from 91 individuals (35 NC, 20 ASD, 36 SZ). Fixation-related potential (FRP) was time-locked to fixation onset. In Experiment 2, fMRI during Guided Search was obtained from a partly overlapping sample of 71 individuals (27 NC, 25 ASD, 19 SZ). In behavioral analyses, SZ was associated with significantly prolonged search time (d=.74, p=.003), which was attributable primarily to reduced mean saccade amplitude, whereas ASD was associated with a small advantage (d=.35), which was not statistically significant. In EEG analyses, SZ was associated with reduced amplitude of the FRP P1 (lambda) response (d=1.15, p<.0001) relative to NC that remained significant following control for saccade size (p<.0001), but with normal task-related modulation of background alpha activity. In contrast, ASD was associated with normal FRP amplitude and larger alpha suppression (d=.83, p=.007) that was attributable to increased alpha levels during pre-task fixation (at matched pre-onset alpha levels, d=.14, p=.66). Within SZ, P1 correlated with the MCCB composite (r=.56, p=.001). Within ASD, ADOS-2 Communication correlated with P1 (r=.51, p=.024) and with the broadband change from pre-onset to search (r=-.51, p=.030). In fMRI, SZ was associated with correlated activation reductions in the Visual1 (Sidak p<.001) and Visual2 (Sidak p=.022) networks and SC (Sidak p=.019), whereas activation was unaffected in the Dorsal Attention and Frontoparietal networks, Frontal Eye Fields and pulvinar. In ASD, activation was increased in pulvinar (Sidak p[≤].038), but unaffected elsewhere. Cortical activation patterns associated with SC activation resembled those associated with P1 generation across groups. Overall, the findings support bottom-up disturbances of visual processing in schizophrenia. In autism, pre-onset alpha was higher and task-related suppression was larger.

title: TRAIT: A Toolbox for Rapid Assembly of Integration Templates for CRISPR/Cas- and Integrase-Mediated Genome Engineering
authors: Timofeev, O.; Hetzel, J.-P.; Abdullah, K.; Schacht, P.
abstract: The generation of genetically engineered mammalian cell models often requires repeated construction of integration donors that differ in their targeting sequences, genetic payloads, or integration strategies. Although modular DNA assembly methods facilitate construct generation, adapting existing expression cassettes to different genome-engineering applications remains labor-intensive. Here, we present TRAIT (Toolbox for Rapid Assembly of Integration Templates), a modular cloning framework that combines direct Golden Gate assembly of targeting elements with Gateway-mediated transfer of genetic payloads. The core vector architecture separates genome-targeting sequences from payload assembly, allowing existing Gateway-compatible constructs to be reused without modification of internal Type IIS restriction sites. We developed vector modules supporting homology-directed repair, homology-independent targeted integration, FrameSelect-compatible donor cleavage, coordinated guide RNA delivery, inducible Cas9 expression, Bxb1-mediated cassette exchange, and conditional transgene expression. An extended MultiSite Gateway workflow enables the assembly of complex integration donors using independently prepared regulatory modules, including components from the Mammalian ToolKit. Functional validation in human cells demonstrated targeted integration, recombinase-mediated cassette exchange, and multiplexed genome editing. We further applied TRAIT to generate human induced pluripotent stem cells carrying functional doxycycline-inducible Cas9 and candidate landing-pad integration constructs. Together, these results establish TRAIT as an interoperable framework for assembling and deploying diverse genome-engineering constructs in mammalian cells.

title: An atlas of the sRNAs and their targets in Staphylococcus aureus
authors: Hussain, F.; Kohl, M. P.; Hou, S.; Lott, S. C.; Ams, E.; Voigt, K.; Lalaouna, D.; Romby, P.; Marzi, S.; Caldelari, I.; Hess, W. R.; Georg, J.
abstract: Small RNAs (sRNAs) control key steps of infection and stress acclimation in the opportunistic pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. Yet most of the more than 250 annotated candidates remain uncharacterized, and even the best-studied have incomplete target spectra. Here we present aureoRNA, an interactive tool that assembles for each sRNA comparative target predictions, available MAPS interactomes, sRNA-mRNA expression correlation across curated public transcriptomes and placement in groups of independently regulated genes (iModulons), and makes these data explorable in one place. GO- and KEGG-based enrichments summarize the datasets at the pathway level for every sRNA, and a weighted rank product combines available data into prioritized target candidate lists. We generated a new MAPS interactome for RsaD and experimentally validated predictions for three sRNAs: new RsaD targets in threonine and arginine catabolism, citZ as an RsaE target, and prophage genes repressed by RNAIII. aureoRNA is a hypothesis-generating resource for the systematic characterization of the sRNA repertoire of this pathogen.

title: Modelling Maternal-to-Zygotic Transition Dynamics to Identify Common Gene Expression Baselines in Zebrafish Development.
authors: grosse Holthaus, M.; Michaelis, P.; Schunck, F.; Focks, A.
abstract: We propose a semi-mechanistic ODE-based transcription model for zebrafish embryogenesis that captures common baseline expression dynamics by integrating the maternal-to-zygotic transition mechanism. We fitted this model to a time-course RNA-seq dataset of D. rerio spanning early developmental stages until 120 hpf. Using the inferred model parameters, we identified common gene expression pattern using fuzzy c-means clustering and compared these with clusters stemming from a shape-based approach using smooth trajectories. We show that the ODE-parameter-based approach improves to biological interpretability by linking clusters to underlying regulatory mechanism, such as the timing of zygotic genome activation, thereby generating more precise expression clusters. However, the results also revealed technical biases of the time-course data, originating from the poly(A) enrichment step.
